lines.text: Temperature change in a calorimeter, $\Delta H$ asked → $Q = mc\Delta T$ with the mass of the water, then $\Delta H = -\frac{Q}{n}$ in kJ, with $n$ the amount of reactant used up; the water warming means $\Delta H$ is negative ({{lesson:4.1}})
$\Delta H$ from an energy profile → products' level minus reactants' level, ignoring the hump; lower products mean exothermic and more stable products ({{lesson:4.1}})
$\Delta H$ from bond enthalpies → bonds broken minus bonds formed (data booklet, section 12), each bond times its coefficient; an estimate, because the values are averages for gases ({{lesson:4.2}})
$\Delta H$ for a target equation from given equations → Hess's law: reverse an equation and change the sign, multiply it and multiply $\Delta H$, then add ({{lesson:4.2}})
Compare fuels → energy per gram $= |\Delta H_\text{c}^\ominus| \div M$; $\ce{CO2}$ per kJ from the moles of $\ce{CO2}$ in the combustion equation ({{lesson:4.5}})

Fuel cell half-equations → fuel oxidized at the negative anode, oxygen reduced at the positive cathode; in acid, balance O with $\ce{H2O}$, H with $\ce{H+}$, then charge with $\ce{e-}$ ({{lesson:4.5}})

$\Delta H^\ominus$ from $\Delta H_\text{f}^\ominus$ data → $\sum$ products $-$ $\sum$ reactants, times coefficients; elements in their standard states are zero, and match $\ce{H2O(l)}$ or $\ce{H2O(g)}$ ({{lesson:4.3}})
$\Delta H^\ominus$ from $\Delta H_\text{c}^\ominus$ data → $\sum$ reactants $-$ $\sum$ products; $\ce{O2}$, $\ce{CO2(g)}$ and $\ce{H2O(l)}$ count as zero ({{lesson:4.3}})

Missing value in a Born–Haber cycle → $\Delta H_\text{f}^\ominus = \sum \Delta H_\text{atom} + \sum \text{IE} + \sum \text{EA} - \Delta H_\text{lattice}$; half the bond enthalpy for a diatomic gas, and count steps twice for two atoms or a $2+$/$2-$ ion ({{lesson:4.4}})
Sign of $\Delta S$ → compare the moles of gas on each side; value of $\Delta S^\ominus$ → $\sum S^\ominus$(products) $-$ $\sum S^\ominus$(reactants), elements included ({{lesson:4.6}})

Is it spontaneous? → $\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$ with $\Delta S^\ominus$ in kJ and $T$ in K, negative means spontaneous; when $\Delta H^\ominus$ and $\Delta S^\ominus$ have the same sign, the crossover is $T = \frac{\Delta H^\ominus}{\Delta S^\ominus}$ ({{lesson:4.7}})

$K$ or which way a mixture reacts, from $\Delta G^\ominus$ → $\Delta G^\ominus = -RT\ln K$ with $\Delta G^\ominus$ in J, so negative $\Delta G^\ominus$ gives $K > 1$; for an actual mixture, $\Delta G = \Delta G^\ominus + RT\ln Q$, negative means it reacts forwards ({{lesson:4.7}})
